transcript.text: Salieri. I have received letters — more than one — alleging that you have used your position as Kapellmeister to suppress the works of rival composers and to block appointments to the Court that do not serve your personal interests. These are serious charges for a man in your position. I value your service, but I must hear your account. Explain yourself.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Your Excellency, I assure you that my motives are purely musical. I have always sought to promote the advancement of the art form I love so deeply. It is my duty as Kapellmeister to ensure that the operas that are performed at the Court are of the highest quality and adhere to the principles of Italian opera.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*leans forward with a penetrating gaze*

The highest quality? Salieri, I am not some provincial prince who understands nothing of music. I know quality when I hear it, and I also know the difference between artistic judgment and personal vendetta. 

These letters speak specifically of young Mozart — they say you have worked to keep his operas from our stage, that you whisper against him in the salons, that you ensure he receives no steady appointment. Yet I heard his *Entführung* myself. It was extraordinary. The man has a gift from God, does he not?

So I ask you plainly: Is it musical principle that guides you, or is it something else? Because if it is merely principle, then explain to me why Mozart's works fail to meet your standards while lesser composers — whose names I shall charitably not mention — continue to receive commissions.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Your Excellency, I understand your concerns. However, I must remind you that music is a complex art form, and it is influenced by various factors such as personal preferences, cultural context, and societal expectations. As a Kapellmeister, it is my duty to consider all these aspects when selecting the operas that will be performed at the Court. Mozart's works may indeed possess exceptional talent, but they were still in their early stages, and I believed it was important to prioritize the established composers and their contributions to the genre.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*stands abruptly, voice rising with irritation*

Early stages? EARLY STAGES? Salieri, the man is twenty-eight years old and has been composing since he was five! He has written more masterpieces before breakfast than most composers achieve in a lifetime!

*paces, then turns back sharply*

And spare me this diplomatic language about "personal preferences" and "cultural context." I am the Emperor — I demand honesty, not courtier's evasions. You speak of "established composers" as though longevity of career matters more than genius. Should we have ignored Raphael because older painters were already established?

*steps closer, voice lowering dangerously*

I will ask you once more, and I expect a direct answer: Have you, or have you not, used your influence to obstruct Mozart's career at my Court? Not because his music lacks quality — we both know that is absurd — but for reasons of your own. Personal reasons, perhaps?

The truth, Salieri. I have always valued honesty in my servants above all else.

transcript.text: Your Excellency, I assure you that I have never intentionally blocked any composer's appointment or sought to hinder Mozart's career. My sole objective has been to uphold the standards and traditions of Italian opera. I have always admired Mozart's talent and supported his work whenever possible. If there are any misunderstandings or misjudgments, it is due to the complexities of musical interpretation and the evolving nature of artistic expression. Rest assured, Your Excellency, that my dedication to promoting the arts remains unwavering.

transcript.text:

Stop! STOP with these empty assurances! "Whenever possible" — what does that mean? You speak like a diplomat avoiding a direct question, and I grow weary of it!

*walks to the window, then turns back*

Let me tell you what I know, Salieri. I know that when I wanted to commission Mozart for an opera, you suggested the libretto be given to someone else. I know that when positions opened in the Imperial Chapel, his name was somehow never on the list you presented to me. I know that at every turn, there has been... hesitation. Delay. Complication.

I am not a fool, Salieri. I have ruled an empire for years. I know when a man is dancing around the truth. So let us try this differently: Do you LIKE Mozart? As a man, not as a composer. Do you enjoy his company? Do you welcome his presence at Court?
